content:
According to reports yesterday, Apple has agreed to comply with the "fairer" App Tracking Transparency (ATT) rules within the EU, following an investigation by the German antitrust watchdog.

Apple stated that it is complying voluntarily, and as far as we understand, a total of eight modifications will be made to meet the relevant requirements……

Developers typically collect far more personal data than required for an app's functionality. The "app tracking" that Apple refers to is one example: the apps you have installed reflect your interests, which are then used to serve you personalised ads, whether within the app or on the web. App Tracking Transparency (ATT) lets you choose whether this data can be collected and used in this way.

Apple said yesterday that the Federal Cartel Office (FCO) recognised the value of offering users a choice; the FCO's report did note that, from a data protection perspective, they welcome the implementation of ATT, and other privacy regulators in the country hold the same position.

The FCO's objection appears to be that Apple's existing prompts make "app tracking" sound more worrying than it actually is. To address this, the iPhone maker will make eight modifications, including removing the word "track".

  • Change the colour of the icon element at the top of the prompt from orange to blue.
  • Update the ATT prompt to a full-page display.
  • Remove the word "track" from both the ATT prompt and the "personalised ads" prompt.
  • Change the ATT option buttons from "Allow" and "Ask App Not to Track" to "Allow" and "Decline".
  • Allow formatting variations (such as bold, italics, and bulleted lists) in the ATT prompt.
  • Add an option for developers to display an additional page of information directly from the prompt to provide further GDPR details. Developers can already actually use their own prompts to display such information before the ATT prompt appears.
  • Allow developers to ask users again with the ATT prompt one year after the user has made a decision, regardless of whether the user selected "Agree" or "Decline" at the time.
  • Make minor wording adjustments to the "personalised ads" prompt for greater clarity, but the effect or meaning of the wording will not change.

Apple told us that they are committed to ensuring ATT continues to be available in EU countries, and said the measure is welcomed by privacy advocacy groups, data protection authorities, and iPhone users.

The company reiterated that its own apps will not display the ATT prompt because they do not use personal data collected from apps to serve targeted ads or measure advertising effectiveness. It stressed that third-party apps are treated in exactly the same way—if a third-party app does not collect this kind of data, it does not need to display a prompt.

9to5Mac Take

This outcome seems to be the best arrangement for everyone. iPhone users can still make a choice, but the prompts they rely on will more accurately reflect the decision they are being asked to make—namely, choosing between "personalised ads" or "not".

This investigation also clarified outside concerns about Apple's own advertising sales business. The company has made it clear that it does not use data collected from its own apps to serve personalised ads, nor to measure advertising effectiveness.
